sentence: The NHS describes psoriasis as a common, long-term skin condition that causes itchy and painful patches of dry, flaky skin.
The main sign is dry, scaly skin, and some people find that it itches or feels sore.
On lighter skin the patches usually look pink or red with silvery-white scales.
On brown and black skin they can look purple or dark brown, with grey scales.
Patches most often appear on the elbows, knees, scalp and lower back.
The NHS also lists the head and behind the ears, the chest, tummy and back, the bottom, the forearms and elbows, and the lower legs and knees as common places.
Psoriasis can also affect the nails, which may develop tiny dents or pits, become discoloured or grow abnormally.
The Psoriasis Association adds that nails grow more quickly in people with psoriasis, and changes can include splitting, or crumbling and thickening of the nail.
The Psoriasis Association lists plaque, scalp, guttate, pustular, inverse and nail psoriasis as the main forms.
It also describes erythrodermic psoriasis and psoriasis in sensitive areas, and says psoriasis can appear on any part of the body.
Its information sheet says psoriasis can range in appearance from mild to severe.
NICE clinical knowledge summaries put plaque psoriasis as the most common type, affecting 80 to 90 percent of people with psoriasis.
note: Search summary: CKS puts plaque share at 80-90%.

sentence: The association says plaques tend to appear on the elbows, knees, lower back and scalp.
It describes scalp psoriasis as one of the most common types and often the first area to show up, sometimes making the scalp feel itchy and tight.
NICE guidance says people with generalised pustular psoriasis or erythroderma should be referred immediately for same-day specialist assessment and treatment.
The NHS explains that psoriasis occurs when skin cells are replaced more quickly than usual.
The cause is not fully known, but it is thought to involve a problem with the immune system.
The Psoriasis Association says overactive T cells of the immune system are implicated in the skin changes.
note: Search summary of PA news article.

sentence: Family history raises the risk, though the exact role of genes is unclear.
Possible triggers listed by the NHS include stress, injury to the skin, some medicines and a throat infection called strep throat.
The NHS also lists drinking alcohol, smoking and obesity.
note: Search summary of NHS causes page.

sentence: The British Association of Dermatologists notes that not everyone who smokes or drinks develops psoriasis.
The Psoriasis Association lists infections, injury to the skin, hormonal changes and certain medicines as triggers.
Diagnosis usually relies on examining the skin, scalp and nails for signs of the condition.
A GP will typically ask when the symptoms appeared and how long they have been present.
A referral to a dermatologist, a specialist skin doctor, may follow if the psoriasis is very severe or there is any doubt about the diagnosis.
note: GOSH: dermatologist described as specialist skin doctor.

sentence: A skin biopsy is very rarely needed.
NICE clinical knowledge summaries advise referral to dermatology if the diagnosis is uncertain, if psoriasis resists topical treatment in primary care, or if treatments are not tolerated.
NHS Scotland's pathway adds that failure of appropriate topical treatment after four weeks warrants routine referral in mild localised disease.
note: Search summary of NHS Scotland pathway.

sentence: The NHS says psoriasis cannot be cured, but treatments can manage the symptoms.
Treatment usually starts with topical products, which are creams and ointments applied to the skin.
The NHS says emollients are moisturising treatments applied directly to the skin to reduce water loss and cover it with a protective film.
For mild psoriasis, an emollient is probably the first treatment a GP will suggest.
NICE clinical knowledge summaries list emollients, corticosteroids, vitamin D analogues, coal tar and short-contact dithranol as topical options, chosen by preference and practicality.
If topical treatment does not work, the NHS says light treatment (phototherapy) or stronger medicines may be needed.
NICE describes ultraviolet B phototherapy as a second-line option.
Systemic medicines such as ciclosporin, methotrexate and acitretin are used for moderate to severe disease.
NHS Scotland notes that when these fail, apremilast or biologic therapies may be needed.
The British Association of Dermatologists says treatment depends on individual circumstances.
The NHS says support from other people with psoriasis, at a local support group or online, can help.
It also notes that national charities offer support and information about psoriasis.
If psoriasis affects mood, the NHS says a GP can refer a person to a mental health specialist.
A Psoriasis Association article on skin care recommends gentle care, lukewarm baths, and avoiding harsh scrubbing or perfumed products.
Newcastle Hospitals dermatology guidance advises against putting fingers into the emollient tub, as this can introduce bacteria and cause infection.
NICE says psoriasis may be associated with psoriatic arthritis, metabolic syndrome, inflammatory bowel disease, anxiety and depression.
The NHS describes psoriatic arthritis as an inflammatory condition that affects the joints.
It says treatment may need to change for people with psoriasis who are planning a baby or are pregnant, as some medicines can be harmful.
